cards.title: Koichiro Miyahara
cards.body: Miyahara was not deciding whether the machine worked; it did, from 9:26 a.m. He was applying the contingency plan's real test: is enough of the market able to take part for price formation to be fair? Only foreign-affiliated brokers said they could re-send orders. He took no market over a partial one.
cards.prompt: 1 October 2020: the Tokyo Stock Exchange's storage is repaired and everything is normal again by 9:26 a.m., with most of the session left. Who decided to stay closed anyway, and which two percentages decided it?
cards.answer: Koichiro Miyahara, TSE president. Firms able to re-send orders came to about 38% of trading value, short of the 50% share of trading value set out in TSE's contingency plan. He decided at the failure response headquarters after an extraordinary Risk Management Committee convened from 11:00 with JPX CEO Kiyota attending; announced at 11:45 a.m.

cards.title: arrowhead stops, for a whole session
cards.sub: 1 October 2020 · Tokyo Stock Exchange and Fujitsu
cards.body: 7:04 a.m. JST: messages showing trouble reading Device 1 of the NAS. 7:55: a memory module has killed its control unit; Device 2 never took over. 8:36: cancel the 9:00 open, all listed issues. 8:54: cut the network, because the normal halt path needs the NAS. 9:26: manual switchover, all functions normal. 11:45: closed for the day.
cards.prompt: One memory module shut a national equity market for an entire session in 2020. Which market and which component, and why did the second device not take over?
cards.answer: The Tokyo Stock Exchange's arrowhead cash equity system, 1 October 2020. A memory module failed in Device 1 of the shared disk device (NAS); at the setting arrowhead ran, automatic switching does not function for a memory-module failure, so the whole NAS went unavailable. Every listed issue was halted; a market Bloomberg sized at $6 trillion lost the day.

cards.title: Report on the Cash Equity Trading System Failure on Oct. 1
cards.sub: 19 October 2020 · Tokyo Stock Exchange, five pages
cards.body: Five pages, published eighteen days after the halt. It states the requirement TSE believed it had, switchover to another device within 30 seconds, explains why the setting chosen with the vendor could not meet it, and ends on the measures, including a council to write resumption rules by March 2021.
cards.prompt: TSE's own report on the October 2020 failure gives two reasons trading could not resume that day: one about machines, one not. What is the second, and what did the vendor's product manual have to do with the failover?
cards.answer: The non-machine reason: TSE 'had no agreement with trading participants on rebooting arrowhead, and had not carried out any tests', and admits a 'lack of rules on how to handle trade resumption after a trading halt in the event of a system failure'. The Fujitsu product manual said automatic switchover would work regardless of the NAS setting; at arrowhead's setting it would not, and the manual's deficiency hid that.

cards.title: The rule that did not exist
cards.body: TSE's Council for Recurrence Prevention Measures reported on 25 March 2021 that the main cause of the failure to resume was an absence of rules, not the hardware. Rules, procedures and drills followed from April 2021. A restart procedure is now part of the market's rulebook, not the operations runbook.
cards.prompt: Since 2021 TSE may reboot arrowhead mid-session to get the market back. Under the rules written after 2020, what happens to an order the exchange is already holding, who must act next, and what survives the reboot?
cards.answer: Orders TSE holds are cancelled when the system is rebooted. Trading participants must in principle re-send the orders their customers gave them, unless a separate agreement with the customer says otherwise. Executions that were processed normally before the suspension stay valid.
